lessons.title: Calculating with signed integers
lessons.summary: Follow changes across zero and determine the sign of a product or quotient.
lessons.objective: Follow changes across zero and determine the sign of a product or quotient.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Draw a short number line for temperatures or levels crossing zero.

Subtract a negative by adding its positive opposite.

Same signs give positive. Different signs give negative.
lessons.method:
Which way should I move?

A positive change moves to the right on a horizontal number line. A negative change moves to the left. Start at the first number and count the change from there.

What does subtracting a negative do?

A negative number tells you a direction. Subtracting that number reverses that direction.

How can I tell the sign before calculating?

For a product or a quotient, deal with the two signs first. Then calculate using the positive magnitudes.
mistakes: A rise changes the temperature by the given amount. It does not give the final temperature directly.
Keep the sign on the starting value. Only the operation with the second value changes.
The rule about matching signs is for multiplication and division. Addition and subtraction use the size and direction of changes.

examples.title: Calculate a signed temperature change
examples.question: A store room starts at \(-4\) °C. Its temperature rises by 9 °C. What is its new temperature?
examples.solution:
Start at \(-4\) and move right by 9 because the temperature rises.

Use 4 of those steps to reach zero. There are 5 steps left.

The calculation is \(-4+9=5\). The new temperature is 5 °C.

examples.title: Subtract a negative number
examples.question: Work out \(-4-(-9)\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Subtracting \(-9\) reverses the effect of adding \(-9\).

Replace the subtraction of a negative by addition: \(-4+9\).

The value is \(5\).

examples.title: Decide the sign of a product or quotient
examples.question: Work out \((-30)\div(-6)\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Both numbers are negative, so the quotient is positive.

On the magnitudes, divide: \(30\div 6=5\).

Put the sign back to obtain \(5\).

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting decimals
lessons.summary: Align place values before adding or subtracting amounts, lengths and prices.
lessons.objective: Align place values before adding or subtracting amounts, lengths and prices.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Line up the units columns, then the tenths and hundredths. Append zeros where needed.

Subtraction keeps the same place values in both rows.

Use pence as whole numbers or keep the decimal points aligned in pounds.
lessons.method:
Why should the decimal points line up?

Temporarily give the numbers the same smallest place value. This lets you add equal-sized units, such as hundredths.

What if a column is empty?

Write a zero so you can see where the missing digit would sit. If needed, exchange one tenth for ten hundredths before subtracting.

How do I check my change?

Prices may have different numbers of displayed digits. Compare and combine them in the same unit before subtracting from the amount paid.
mistakes: Adding a zero at the end of the fractional part keeps the value unchanged. Moving the decimal point changes it.
Start at the smallest place. Regroup from the next place to the left if needed.
Add the total and your change. The result should be the amount paid.

examples.title: Align decimal places
examples.question: Work out \(3.7+1.51\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Put tenths below tenths and hundredths below hundredths.

Write both numbers as hundredths: 370 and 151. Add these as whole numbers.

The sum is 521 hundredths, or \(5.21\).

examples.title: Subtract decimals with a missing place
examples.question: Work out \(6-1.71\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Write \(6.00\) so the hundredths are visible.

Subtract 171 hundredths from 600 hundredths.

429 hundredths is \(4.29\).

examples.title: Work out change for two items
examples.question: A customer pays £15 for a sketchpad costing £2.58 and a pen costing £1.50. Find the change in pounds.
examples.solution:
Add the two prices in pence: 258 p and 150 p.

The total cost is £4.08. Subtract it from £15.

The change is £10.92.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals
lessons.summary: Scale decimals to whole counts and check the size of the result.
lessons.objective: Scale decimals to whole counts and check the size of the result.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Tenths times hundredths give thousandths. Powers of ten used in both factors affect the product.

Choose a power of ten that makes the divisor whole.

Check whether the story asks for one piece, all pieces or the remainder.
lessons.method:
Where does the decimal point go?

Represent each factor as an integer count of tenths or hundredths. Multiply those counts and put back the place value of their product.

How can I make the divisor easier?

A quotient compares two numbers. Multiplying both by an equal non-zero scale leaves the quotient unchanged.

How do I use a repeated decimal length?

Write the measurements in the same unit. Multiply to find the full amount used, then subtract if the question asks what remains.
mistakes: The product of two positive decimals below 1 is smaller than either one.
Scaling only the divisor changes the answer.
Keep enough precision to finish the exact decimal calculation.

examples.title: Multiply decimals with different lengths
examples.question: Work out \(1.5\times0.07\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
The first factor has 15 tenths. The second has 7 hundredths.

Multiply the integer counts: \(15\times7=105\). Tenths times hundredths give thousandths.

The product is \(0.105\).

examples.title: Make the divisor a whole number
examples.question: Work out \(0.3\div0.05\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Think of the division as \(\frac{0.3}{0.05}\).

Multiply both numbers by 100, so the calculation becomes \(30\div 5\).

The answer is 6. Check that 6 copies of \(0.05\) make \(0.3\).

examples.title: Find the length left over
examples.question: 6 pieces, each 0.18 m long, are cut from a 2.8 m ribbon. Find the length of ribbon left.
examples.solution:
Find the total removed length by multiplying 6 by \(0.18\).

The pieces use \(1.08\) m. Subtract from the original \(2.8\) m.

The remaining length is \(1.72\) m.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
lessons.summary: Use equal-sized parts before combining fractions and mixed numbers.
lessons.objective: Use equal-sized parts before combining fractions and mixed numbers.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Rewrite both fractions with a common denominator. Then add only the counts on top.

Subtract the numerators in the order given. Simplify at the end.

Use one common denominator for both complete numbers.
lessons.method:
Why do the denominators have to match?

A denominator tells you the size of the pieces. If two fractions use different sizes, split their bars into equal-size pieces before adding.

How do I subtract parts of the same whole?

Draw equal bars to compare what remains. Once the parts match in size, subtract the number of those parts.

What if there is a whole part as well?

A mixed number has a whole part and a fractional part. Rename each whole in the same-sized pieces before subtracting.
mistakes: The denominator stays as the common size. Adding the denominators changes the size of every piece.
Check the sign. The result can be negative if you subtract a larger value.
Keep the value of the whole part when converting to an improper fraction.

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{2}{5}+\frac{2}{7}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 35.

Write \(\frac{14}{35}+\frac{10}{35}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{24}{35}\).

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 8.

Write \(\frac{4}{8}-\frac{3}{8}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{1}{8}\).

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(1\,\frac{1}{7}-\frac{4}{9}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 63.

Write \(\frac{72}{63}-\frac{28}{63}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{44}{63}\).

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
lessons.summary: Find a fraction of a fraction and use the reciprocal when dividing.
lessons.objective: Find a fraction of a fraction and use the reciprocal when dividing.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply the counts on top and the sizes on bottom, then simplify the result.

Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. Keep the first fraction the same.

Convert any mixed number before applying the reciprocal rule.
lessons.method:
What is a part of a part?

Shade some columns of a grid for one fraction and some rows for another. The overlap shows the product as part of the whole.

Why does division use the reciprocal?

Dividing asks how many copies of one number fit into another. If the divisor is a fraction, its reciprocal tells you how many of those pieces make one whole.

How do I divide when a number is mixed?

Rename the whole part and fraction as one improper fraction. Then use the usual division steps.
mistakes: A product of proper positive fractions should be smaller than its factors.
Only invert the second fraction, the number you are dividing by.
For written work, use the final fraction or mixed form requested in the question.

examples.title: Multiply fractions in exact form
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{2}{5}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.

Before simplifying, the product is \(\frac{2}{15}\).

If the numerator and denominator share a factor greater than 1, cancel it. The result is \(\frac{2}{15}\).

examples.title: Divide by a fraction
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{4}{9}\div \frac{3}{5}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Dividing by the second number is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal \(\frac{5}{3}\).

Use \(\frac{4}{9}\times \frac{5}{3}\). Keep the first fraction in its original order.

The result in simplest form is \(\frac{20}{27}\).

examples.title: Divide a mixed number
examples.question: Work out \(5\,\frac{1}{9}\div \frac{3}{10}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Rewrite the whole number and fraction together as \(\frac{46}{9}\).

Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor: \(\frac{46}{9}\times \frac{10}{3}\).

The result is \(\frac{460}{27}\). Convert to a mixed number if the question asks for one.

lessons.title: Order of operations and brackets
lessons.summary: Identify each group and work in the order shown by the notation.
lessons.objective: Identify each group and work in the order shown by the notation.
lessons.before: Make a rough estimate, then test the method in the first example.
lessons.ideas:
Start inside brackets. Then do powers and roots, products and quotients, and finally sums and differences.

Treat division and multiplication as equal priority. Start with whichever is earlier in the line.

Find the value on top and the value below before dividing.
lessons.method:
What should I work out first?

Brackets group a small calculation inside a bigger one. Finish the inner group before applying the operation outside it.

What if the two operations have equal priority?

Multiplication and division share one level. Addition and subtraction share another. Within one level, go from left to right.

Where are the hidden brackets?

A fraction bar groups everything written above it and everything below it. A root bar also shows exactly what goes inside its own operation.
mistakes: Writing the next line one step at a time makes it easier to spot which operation is next.
The order of letters in a mnemonic does not make division always come first.
On a calculator, put brackets around an entire numerator or denominator when using the division key.

examples.title: Use the brackets first
examples.question: Work out \(5+3\times(4+2)\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Calculate the bracket first: 4 plus 2 is 6.

Then multiply 3 by 6 to get 18.

Add 5, giving 23.

examples.title: Work across equal-priority operations
examples.question: Work out \(20\div 5\times 4\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
Division and multiplication have equal priority. Read this line from left to right.

Start with \(20\div 5=4\).

Then \(4\times 4=16\).

examples.title: Treat a fraction bar as grouping
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{8+6^2}{7-2}\) without a calculator.
examples.solution:
The numerator and denominator are separate calculations.

The numerator is 44; the denominator is 5.

Divide to find \(\frac{44}{5}\).

1. A customer pays £70 for a sketchpad costing £4.33 and a pen costing £2.55. Find the change in pounds.

    Show the method you used.

    [2]

  2. Work out \(29.4-4.44\) without a calculator.

    Show the method you used.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Add the two prices in pence: 433 p and 255 p.

The total cost is £6.88. Subtract it from £70.

The change is £63.12.

(b)

Write \(29.40\) so the hundredths are visible.

Subtract 444 hundredths from 2940 hundredths.

2496 hundredths is \(24.96\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the prices before subtracting from the amount paid.

(b)

You can subtract using hundredths as the unit. Write a zero in a blank place.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the total cost and subtract it from the amount paid, or subtract each cost in turn.
Align corresponding place values or express both values as counts of hundredths before subtracting.
